No, honestly... no, not at all. It’s actually really frustrating because... well, most days I wake up with this just... this flat, heavy sadness. Right from the second I open my eyes, it's just sitting there. And I used to have these things, these activities that would sort of reset me, you know? Like a palate cleanser for my brain after a long week of dealing with frustrated users and broken servers. 

I’ve got this pretty extensive vinyl collection—mostly vintage jazz and some 70s prog rock—and I used to love just picking out a record, cleaning the dust off, dropping the needle, and really actively listening to it. Or cooking. I used to spend my whole Sunday afternoon making a proper ragu from scratch, letting it simmer for hours, chopping all the fresh herbs... or tinkering with electronics. That was a really big one for me. I have this little workbench setup in the apartment where I build custom mechanical keyboards and mess around with microcontrollers. I used to get so absorbed in soldering the little components, getting the switches just right, testing the circuits. It was so satisfying to fix something and see it work.

Well, um... no, I don't have a plan or anything like that. I'm not sitting here figuring out how to, you know, actually do something to myself. But... Well, yeah, actually. It's... it's funny you ask that because I was just thinking about this the other day when I was trying to get through the ticket queue. Well, um... yeah, actually. It's... it's kind of hard to talk about because I know how it sounds, and working in IT, you know, I'm used to things having a logical explanation, a root cause that you can trace back and fix. But lately, especially since I moved into this smaller apartment after the pipe burst at the old place... some nights, it gets really weird. 

It usually happens when it's super quiet, like after 2:00 AM, when the street noise dies down and I'm just lying there trying to sleep, staring at the ceiling. I'll start hearing this... this dripping sound. Like water hitting a puddle. And at first, I thought, "Great, another plumbing issue," because of what happened at the last place, you know? So I'd get up and check the kitchen sink, the bathroom, the radiator, everywhere. But it's bone dry. And the dripping doesn't sound like it's coming from the pipes anyway. It sounds like it's coming from the corner of the living room, right where I have all my old vinyl records boxed up. I haven't unpacked them because there's just no space here, and honestly, I haven't had the energy to set up the turntable anyway. 

But it's not just the dripping. That's the thing. Sometimes... sometimes mixed in with that dripping sound, I'll hear a voice. A really low, muffled voice, kind of like it's coming through a wall or a bad headset connection. And it's saying my name. Just... my name, over and over, really slowly. The first time it happened, I actually walked over to the boxes and stood there in the dark, just listening, trying to figure out if it was a neighbor or someone outside the window, because this place is on the ground floor. But the sound was coming from *inside* the room. From the boxes. And it sounds so incredibly real. I mean, I know it can't be real—there's nobody there, there's no water, it's just cardboard and old records—but in that moment, it sounds as clear as you and me talking right now. It really freaks me out, to be honest. I end up just putting my noise-canceling headphones on and playing white noise until the sun comes up, because I just can't deal with it.

Well, um... that's... that's the thing that really messes with my head, honestly. Because, like I said, I work in IT. My entire job, my whole career, is based on logic. If a server is down, there's a reason. If a script fails, there's a syntax error or a permission issue. There's always a root cause. So, the logical part of my brain—the part that troubleshoots network latency and active directory syncs all day—that part tells me, "No, obviously there isn't a tiny person trapped in a box of old Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd records calling your name." I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I know how the world works. I know that voices don't just spontaneously generate from cardboard and vinyl in a dry room. 

But... but then there's the other part. The part of me that's actually lying there in the dark at 3:00 AM, when the white noise generator is off and the street is completely dead. And in those moments... God, it feels so real. It sounds as real as the hum of my refrigerator or the traffic out on the avenue during rush hour. It has texture, you know? Like, I can hear the breath behind the word. I can hear the slight distortion, like I mentioned, like a bad VoIP call where the packets are dropping just a little bit, but you can still make out exactly what the person is saying. And it's saying my name. It's not just random noise that my brain is trying to make sense of, like pareidolia for audio or whatever. It's specifically calling for me. 

So, do I believe it's real? In the daylight, sitting here in this office, looking out the window at the normal world? No, I know it's not real. I know it's some kind of glitch in my own hardware, a misfiring synapse or whatever. But when it's happening... when I'm standing there in my bare feet on the cold hardwood floor, staring at those moving boxes in the corner, and I hear that low, muffled voice... in that exact second, I believe it. I absolutely believe it's there. And that's what terrifies me, honestly. That I can know something is impossible, but still experience it as completely, undeniably real. It makes me question everything else, you know? Like, if my brain can fake that so perfectly, what else is it faking?

I don't know, none of it reaches me anymore. I try, I really do. I’ll sit at the workbench and look at the circuit boards, or I'll stare at my record shelves, and it’s just... nothing. It just feels like a massive chore. The music just sounds like background noise now, so I don't even bother turning the amplifier on. And the thought of cooking just completely exhausts me, so I just eat whatever is in a wrapper. That heavy sadness just kind of blankets all of it, and the things that used to make me feel like myself, the things that used to bring me back to baseline... they just don't work anymore. I just end up sitting there, feeling exactly as flat and empty as I did when I woke up.\n\nDoctor: Have you had thoughts of harming yourself?\n\nPatient: Well, um... no, I don't have a plan or anything like that. I'm not sitting here figuring out how to, you know, actually do something to myself. But... I mean, if I'm being completely honest, and I guess that's why I'm here, right? To be honest about all this... I do catch myself having these thoughts. A lot, actually. \n\nIt's usually when I'm lying in bed at night, looking up at the ceiling, just dreading the next day. Dreading having to face the ticket queue, dreading having to see my coworkers and know they're carrying my weight. And I just think... I think it would just be so much easier if I just didn't wake up. Like, if my heart just stopped in my sleep or something. It wouldn't be me doing it, it would just happen. And then... well, then it would just be over. The guilt, the heavy feeling, the mess in the apartment. All of it. \n\nAnd more than that, I think about how it would be easier for everyone else, too. Because right now, I feel like this massive burden. I feel like I'm just this anchor dragging my team down, dragging everyone around me down. And if I just wasn't here... if I just quietly slipped away in my sleep... then nobody would have to deal with me anymore. They could hire someone who actually does the job right, who doesn't let the tickets pile up. My landlord could clear out the apartment and rent it to someone who actually cleans. It just... it feels like the math works out better if I'm just not in the equation, you know? But no, I wouldn't do it myself. I don't have a plan to hurt myself. It's just this constant, lingering wish that I could just... disappear.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this heavy sadness and guilt?\n\nPatient: Well, um... let me think. It’s been a while now. I’d say... yeah, it’s been about a year and two months. I remember exactly when it started, actually, because it was right around the time I had to move. \n\nSee, I used to live in this great place over on 4th Street. It had this big window where the afternoon light would come in right onto my workbench, which was perfect for soldering because you really need good light for that, you know? But then, in the middle of winter, a pipe burst in the unit above mine. It was a complete disaster. Water came pouring through the ceiling, ruined a bunch of my vintage jazz records—I lost an original pressing of 'Kind of Blue' that I had hunted down at a flea market, which just broke my heart. \n\nAnyway, the building management had to do all this remediation, pulling out drywall and everything, so they moved me into a different unit on the ground floor. But it’s so much smaller, and it’s dark, and I couldn't set up my workbench the same way. I couldn't organize my records. My whole routine just completely fell apart. I couldn't come home and unwind the way I used to. And that’s when it started, really. That’s when the heavy feeling just sort of moved in with me into that new apartment. I thought it was just the stress of the move at first, you know? Dealing with the insurance and the damaged stuff and trying to figure out where to put my keyboard parts in a place with half the closet space. But the boxes just stayed packed, and the feeling never left. It just kept getting heavier and heavier, and spreading into my work, and now here we are, a year and two months later, and I just... I can't shake it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels or how quickly you move and react to things?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, actually. It's... it's funny you ask that because I was just thinking about this the other day when I was trying to get through the ticket queue. It's like... you know when you're trying to use a remote desktop connection to fix a user's machine, and their internet is just terrible, so there's this massive lag between when you click the mouse and when the cursor actually moves on their screen? That's exactly how my body feels right now. \n\nLike, at work, I'll be sitting there, and I know exactly what I need to type to resolve a simple password reset or a printer mapping issue—stuff I've done a thousand times, stuff I could usually do in my sleep. But my hands will just... hover over the keyboard. I'll just sit there staring at the keys, and it's like the signal from my brain is just taking forever to reach my fingers. It takes me so much longer to answer even the most basic support tickets now. \n\nAnd it's not just typing, it's everything. Getting out of a chair feels like I'm moving underwater. Even just turning my head when someone calls my name from the next cubicle... I know I'm reacting slowly, I can feel it happening, but I can't speed it up. It's like my brain and my body are running on this awful, delayed connection, and the latency is just getting worse and worse. I used to be the guy who could juggle three chat windows and a phone call all at once, typing ninety words a minute, and now... now I'm just staring at my hands, waiting for them to do what I'm telling them to do. It's exhausting, honestly. Just the physical act of moving through the day feels like it takes twice the energy it used to.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?\n\nPatient: Weight? Um... well, no, not really. I mean, I guess I haven't really been paying that much attention to it, to be honest. It's not like I have a scale in my apartment or anything. I used to have one, actually, back at the old place on 4th Street, this nice digital one with the glass top, but it got smashed when they were moving my stuff out after the pipe burst. It's just... everything else feels so heavy, you know? It's kind of like that, but... deeper. And darker, I guess. \n\nI just catch myself thinking that it would be so much easier if I just went to sleep and didn't wake up. Like, if my system just naturally powered down and didn't reboot. And then there's the guilt, feeling like I'm letting my team down because my ticket resolution time has tanked, and I'm just a burden to everyone around me. If I just wasn't here... if I just faded out in my sleep... then nobody would have to deal with me anymore. The team could hire someone who actually has the energy to do the job right, and my landlord could rent this dark little ground-floor apartment to someone who doesn't mind it, and I wouldn't have to feel this... this crushing heaviness every single second of the day. So, yeah, no plans, no intent to make it happen myself. Just... a really strong wish for an automatic shutdown, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any strange or unusual thoughts, like hearing voices or seeing things that others can't?\n\nPatient: Well, um... yeah, actually. It's... it's kind of hard to talk about because I know how it sounds, and working in IT, you know, I'm used to things having a logical explanation, a root cause that you can trace back and fix. But lately, especially since I moved into this smaller apartment after the pipe burst at the old place... some nights, it gets really weird. \n\nIt usually happens when it's super quiet, like after 2:00 AM, when the street noise dies down and I'm just lying there trying to sleep, staring at the ceiling. So I'd get up and check the kitchen sink, the bathroom, the radiator, everywhere. But it's bone dry. And the dripping doesn't sound like it's coming from the pipes anyway. It sounds like it's coming from the corner of the living room, right where I have all my old vinyl records boxed up. Just stupid stuff, honestly, like miscategorizing a hardware request, or maybe taking too long to escalate a tier-2 network issue because I'm so tired, or forgetting to log my resolution notes before closing a ticket. 

My coworkers, they're great, and they keep telling me, "Hey man, don't worry about it, it's fine. Everyone messes up, those ticket errors are totally normal, especially with the new system update we just rolled out." They try to brush it off and tell me my metrics are still fine. But I just... I can't accept that. I get completely stuck on this idea—this absolute certainty, really—that the company is quietly tracking every single mistake I make. 

Like, I'm convinced there's a hidden dashboard somewhere, or some silent audit log that management and HR are reviewing every Friday afternoon behind closed doors. I just know they are building this massive, air-tight case to fire me. Because they’ve figured it out. They’ve figured out that I’m basically a fraud. That I don't actually know what I'm doing, that my degree is useless, and I've just been faking it this whole time. 

And I'll sit there at my desk, looking at the ticket queue, and every time an email pings from my supervisor, even if the subject line is just about a team lunch or a software patch, my stomach completely drops. Because my brain immediately goes, "This is it. This is the calendar invite for the meeting where they show you the logs, expose you, and walk you out of the building with your stuff in a cardboard box." 

So when I hear that voice at night, calling my name from the corner of the room... it just feels like an extension of that same feeling. Like the universe, or whatever is in those boxes, is just echoing what management already knows. That I'm a fake, and I'm caught, and my time is up. I just can't shake that belief, no matter how much logical evidence my team gives me that I'm doing fine. It's exhausting, honestly, just waiting for the axe to fall every single minute of the day.

Well, um... like I was saying before, about how it happens in this new, smaller apartment... when I hear that water dripping, or that low voice saying my name, it really doesn't feel like it's inside my head. It feels entirely outside of me. And I think about this a lot, because, you know, when I'm troubleshooting an audio issue on a user's machine at work, the first thing I do is isolate the source. Is it the internal speakers? Is it an external peripheral? Is there interference? 

So I try to apply that same diagnostic logic to myself. When I'm lying there, and the voice starts up, it has actual directional audio. It's not echoing inside my skull the way my own thoughts do, or the way a song gets stuck in your head. It is specifically originating from that boxed-up corner where my records are. If I turn my head on the pillow, the sound shifts in my ears, exactly the way a real, physical noise in the room would. 

That's why I always end up getting out of bed to check. Because it sounds so completely real at the time that my brain processes it as external audio data. I'll walk right up to those cardboard boxes, half expecting to find a speaker someone hid there as a prank, or a leak from the ceiling hitting the vinyl, but... there's nothing. Absolutely nothing there. 

So, logically, sitting here talking to you, I have to conclude that it’s a part of my own mind. It has to be, right? Because the physical evidence proves there is no external source. But it just... it doesn't *behave* like a thought. It behaves like a sound wave bouncing off the walls of my apartment. I've even caught myself thinking about bringing home a high-end condenser microphone from the AV department at work, just to record the room overnight. Just so I can look at the waveform on my monitor the next morning and have visual, hard data proving that the room was silent. Because my own senses are betraying me so thoroughly. It’s just so hard to accept that my own mind can fabricate something that feels so entirely outside of myself, right down to the acoustics of the room.
